subject: music
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Use of musical elements and structure

questions.q: What percentage of the total AQA GCSE Music (8271) qualification is Component 3: Composing Music worth?
questions.explain: Component 3 accounts for 30% of the GCSE, with the remaining 70% split between the listening exam and performing.

questions.q: How is Component 3: Composing Music assessed?
questions.explain: Composing is coursework marked by the centre and moderated by AQA, making it a non-exam assessment.

questions.q: How many separate compositions must a student submit for Component 3?
questions.explain: Students submit two compositions: one to a brief and one free composition.

questions.q: Composition 1 must be written in response to what?
options: A brief chosen by the student
A poem selected by the teacher
A brief written by the exam moderator
questions.explain: Composition 1 is the 'composition to a brief', where the brief is provided by AQA.

questions.q: What is the name given to Composition 2 in Component 3?
questions.explain: Composition 2 is the free composition, in which the student explores their own musical ideas.

questions.q: What is the minimum combined duration of the two compositions?
questions.explain: The two compositions together must last a minimum of three minutes.

questions.q: How many marks are available in total for Component 3?
questions.explain: Each composition is worth 40 marks, giving a total of 80 marks for the component.

questions.q: How many marks is each individual composition worth?
questions.explain: Both the composition to a brief and the free composition are each marked out of 40.

questions.q: Who is responsible for setting the brief used for Composition 1?
questions.explain: For the composition to a brief, AQA provides the briefs to which students respond.

questions.q: For the free composition, who decides the style, mood and starting point of the piece?
questions.explain: The free composition allows the student to set their own brief and choose their own musical direction.

questions.q: How are the AQA composition briefs connected to the rest of the course?
options: Each brief is linked to one of the four areas of study
Each brief is based on a single set work
Each brief must use a named composer's melody
Each brief specifies an exact key and time signature
questions.explain: The briefs relate to the four areas of study, connecting composing to the wider course content.

questions.q: In addition to an audio recording, what must be submitted for each composition?
options: A programme note about a composer
questions.explain: Each composition is submitted as a recording accompanied by a score or a written annotation of the music.

questions.q: Which letters correctly represent the structure of ternary form?
questions.explain: Ternary form has three sections, with the opening material returning after a contrasting middle section (ABA).

questions.q: Which structure is described as binary form?
questions.explain: Binary form consists of two sections, usually labelled A and B.

questions.q: Which of the following is a musical element a composer manipulates when writing music?
questions.explain: Harmony is a musical element, alongside melody, rhythm, texture, dynamics and tonality, whereas the others are genres, ensembles or features.

questions.q: What is the main way the free composition differs from the composition to a brief?
options: It does not need a recording
The student sets their own brief and chooses the style
It is marked out of 20 rather than 40
It must be at least five minutes long
questions.explain: Unlike the AQA-set brief, the free composition lets the student decide the stimulus, genre and approach for themselves.

questions.q: A student wants complete freedom over the genre, instrumentation and mood of a piece. Which composition allows this?
options: Neither, as both are set by AQA
Both are decided by the teacher
questions.explain: The free composition gives the student full control over style, resources and expressive intent.

questions.q: A student's two finished compositions last 1 minute 20 seconds and 1 minute 30 seconds. Do they meet the duration requirement?
options: Yes, because each lasts over a minute
Yes, because there are two pieces
No, because the combined total is under three minutes
No, because each must last three minutes
questions.explain: The two pieces total 2 minutes 50 seconds, which falls short of the required minimum combined duration of three minutes.

questions.q: A composer writes a piece with a main theme that keeps returning between contrasting episodes, giving the structure ABACA. Which form is this?
questions.explain: Rondo form features a recurring main theme (A) alternating with contrasting episodes, such as ABACA.

questions.q: A student wants an opening section, a contrasting middle, and then a return of the opening material. Which structure best fits this plan?
questions.explain: Ternary form provides exactly this shape, with the A material returning after a contrasting B section.
